noi_dung:
Cultivate Genuinely; Do Not Be Lax

Gold Mountain Monastery was formerly called the Buddhist Lecture Hall, located on the fourth floor of an apartment building in San Francisco's Chinatown, and was established by the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association. The first summer study session was held here in 1968. At that time a great many people came from Seattle to join that 96-day session. The study schedule was very demanding, with no rest each day; only Saturday afternoons were free, for laundry or personal matters.

During that session I lectured on the Shurangama Sutra, planning to finish before the session ended. At first I lectured once a day, but after a while I saw we would not meet the deadline, so I increased it to twice a day. Gradually, still fearing we could not finish, I raised it to three times a day; and in the end it became four times a day. And so, in that summer session the Shurangama Sutra was completed, with its perfected merit dedicated to all beings.

After the Shurangama Sutra lectures ended, five young American men and women sought to leave home. These were the first Americans to leave home and receive the Complete Precepts—three Bhikshus and two Bhikshunis.

Afterward, every year there has been a summer study session. A great many people came to study the Buddhadharma, and many left home to become Bhikshus and Bhikshunis. Though the numbers were not large, for Gold Mountain Monastery—which values quality, not quantity—genuine cultivation and study of the Buddhadharma is what matters: even one person is not too few, let alone that there were more than one or two!

Each month Gold Mountain Monastery publishes a bilingual Chinese-English magazine—Vajra Bodhi Sea. This magazine presents the essential meaning of the Buddhadharma so that Westerners can understand the origins of Buddhism and gain a correct understanding of the Buddhadharma, and no longer regard Buddhism as superstition, idol worship, negativity, pessimism, or a "parasite" on society. This magazine shows people that Buddhism means freedom and equality, with the goal of promoting world peace, and that everyone alike is a disciple of the Buddha—with absolutely no barriers of race, nationality, or territory. Since its beginnings, Buddhism has never caused a war, because the very first precept of Buddhist morality is No Killing—not only must one not kill people, one must not kill even animals; on the contrary, one frees and protects all living creatures—and so no wars are ever caused!

Gold Mountain Monastery is like a place that "sifts sand in search of gold"—if you are "gold," then when you come to Gold Mountain Monastery you will feel as if it were your own home. Here, no one chats, so it is very convenient for reading—studying the Buddhadharma day after day, disturbed by no one—truly an ideal setting! Though Americans are many, how many sincerely resolve to come here to study the Buddhadharma, to hear Sutras and learn the Dharma? Thus, becoming a Buddha depends on the individual, not on the group. In this world, whatever is rare is precious—though the number studying the Buddhadharma at Gold Mountain Monastery is small, to this world it is incomparably precious! In the future, once you have penetrated the Buddhadharma, you can go everywhere to propagate it, benefit beings, and lead all beings to soon accomplish the Buddha Way—that is what I expect of you!

In this summer session, everyone must treasure time and let none of it go to waste. There is a saying:

"An inch of time is an inch of gold,

But an inch of gold cannot redeem an inch of time."

Time, then, is the most precious, the most important thing. All of you joining this year's summer session, strive to learn the Buddhadharma; do not let time slip by in vain—you must surely learn some true principle.

There is something I wish to tell you. Truly I did not want to say it, but now I cannot remain silent. What is it? Those who have left home must know self-respect: do not think too lowly of yourselves, yet do not be arrogant and conceited either; always reflect and examine yourselves—if you have made any mistake, correct it at once; if you are faultless, advance further; absolutely do not be careless, lax, or indulgent.

Once you are my left-home disciples, whenever I see a fault in you I will surely point it out so you may know and correct it. If I did not speak, I would truly be failing you. Once I have spoken what I have seen, whether you listen or not, whether you reform or not—that is your affair. I only fulfill a teacher's duty, with a clear conscience. Do not wait until you have fallen into the hells to blame your Master: "Oh! Why didn't my Master teach me more strictly at the start? Had he taught me more carefully, more sternly, how could I have fallen into the hells?"

Now I have said what I wished to say; those of you who have left home must remember: you must not disturb or interfere with the freedom of others, nor affect their actions. If you yourself do not wish to cultivate, so be it—but do not obstruct the cultivation of others; if you yourself do not uphold the precepts, do not hinder others from upholding them; if you yourself do not foster virtue, do not block others from refining their virtue! Whoever harbors such thoughts and conduct must reform at once, "turning evil into good." Those who have left home must watch over themselves every second, every minute—every word, every deed must always accord with the precepts. You must be earnest, never indulgent or undisciplined; you may not do whatever you please. There is a saying:

Without rules, no square or circle can be made.

(Without standards, nothing square or round can be formed.)

Thus, when the Buddha was about to enter Nirvana, he instructed Venerable Ananda: "Take the precepts as your teacher!" That is what those who have left home must engrave upon their hearts.

When eating, we must remember the Three Recollections and the Five Contemplations, for:

A single grain of rice from a donor

Is heavy as Mount Sumeru.

Having eaten it, if you do not cultivate,

You will repay it wearing fur and horns.

(A single grain of a donor's rice

Weighs as much as Mount Sumeru.

Eat it and fail to cultivate,

And you will repay it bearing fur and horns.)

It is that dreadful, that dangerous, all of you! This is called "losing the human body right beneath the kasaya robe"! Therefore, those who have left home, wherever they are, must strictly uphold the precepts—until birth and death are ended and the mind of sexual desire is severed, never for a moment be lazy, lax, or indulgent. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva teaches:

"A day has passed, and life likewise decreases,

Like a fish in shallow water—what joy is there in that?

Great assembly!

Be vigorous and diligent, as if your head were ablaze;

Remember impermanence always, and never be lax!"

We who have left home must treasure every second and minute; remember that:

"An inch of time is an inch of gold, yet an inch of gold cannot redeem an inch of time."

Time is so precious that we must not waste it. Everyone must apply effort in cultivation, ever more vigorously, if accomplishment is to be hoped for. Those who truly apply effort have no time for gossip about others' rights and wrongs, no time for scattered busyness that interrupts cultivation. On this point, I hope everyone will take heed.

When I see people unwilling to cultivate, I feel boundless grief—for have they not failed to carry out the vows they made at the very start, when they first left home to cultivate? Can those who have left home yet whose "minds think one thing while their mouths say another" be worthy of the Sangha Jewel? I hope you will all know self-respect!
